title.text: Cloud reported over the Bay of Naples, noticed at Misenum

when_source.text: Pliny, Letters 6.16 §4, gives a Roman calendar date and “about the seventh hour”.

conversion.text: 24 August, Julian calendar — our conversion of the checked page’s reading. The letter gives the ninth day before the Kalends of September; counting back inclusively with 1 September as day one, the ninth day is 24 August. No Gregorian or proleptic date is given.

hour.as_given: “about the seventh hour”, as Pliny gives it.
hour.model: Our model: Roman hours divided daylight into twelve seasonal hours, so the seventh hour began at local midday.
hour.clock: Modern clock time: unset — daylight at Misenum on that date was not established.

year.text: Year: not stated by this source (the whole letter, §1–22, was checked).

place.reference: Bay of Naples — our present-day reference.

reports.text: Pliny reports that his mother pointed out the cloud to his uncle, who commanded the fleet at Misenum (§4).
He writes that it was learned later that the cloud came from Vesuvius (§5).

caveat.text: Pliny says he set down what he witnessed and what he heard soon afterwards, without saying which details are which (§22).

uncertain.text: Written after his uncle’s death; how long after is not stated (§1).

scholarly_note.text: D’Auria, De Micco & Di Pasquale’s abstract reports that the classical reading of Pliny’s account gives 24 August, and describes a proposal by some scholars to date the eruption to 24 October instead; it suggests the discrepancy is probably a medieval copying error. It refers to the eruption as AD 79; that year is the abstract’s statement, not Pliny’s.
